meta.source: temp/a23-fulltext/{WID}.txt, produced by 240 from the retrieved files; plus abstracts recovered at 5a and 5f for records whose full text is not on disk.
meta.rule: One row per reported effect, not per study. `evidence` quotes the sentence the number was read from, so every row can be checked against the text without re-reading the paper.
meta.not_verified: No second extractor. The acceptance criterion asks the RA to verify a random 10%; that has not been done and the chapter must say so.

effects.config_basis: sample restriction — households observed with and without a co-resident grandparent
effects.arrangement_measure: presence of grandparent(s) in the household
effects.evidence: the presence of grandparent(s) in a household has a positive impact on the number of children born (particularly when both grandparents are present), with estimates ranging from 0.0771 (95% CI: 0.0175 to 0.1368) for both grandparents to 0.1373 (95% CI: 0.0824 to 0.1922) overall
effects.note: Fixed effects remove time-invariant household unobservables. They do NOT address the anticipation problem in scope §3: a household that expects a birth may take a grandparent in. The paper runs a lead model for reverse causation, which is the right instinct and is not an exclusion restriction.

effects.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
effects.setting: Mosuo and neighbouring populations, SW China (matrilineal)
effects.arrangement_measure: post-marital residence: own parents / husband's parents / both / neither
effects.estimate: HR 1.306 (own parents only vs husband's parents only); HR 1.746 (both sets)
effects.evidence: women who resided with their own parents only had earlier AFB than those living with only their husband's parents (HR = 1.306), while those living with both sets of parents had still earlier births (HR = 1.746)
effects.note: THE DIRECTION OF THE CONTRAST IS WITHIN THE EXTENDED CELL, not extended versus independent. It says whose parents matter, which is Amendment 2's point, and it cannot be read as an effect of co-residence itself.

effects.config_basis: sample restriction — married women co-residing with husband's parents
effects.n: Taiwan Panel Study of Family Dynamics; older cohort 1933-1954, younger 1955-1968
effects.anticipation_control: co-residence and labour supply treated as ENDOGENOUS; full-information maximum likelihood duration model with endogenous binary variables
effects.estimate: CORRECTED (FIML, both decisions endogenous): duration to first birth LONGER among co-residing women by 16.2% (coef 0.150), about 4.6 months, older cohort; and by 102.6% (coef 0.706), about 30.6 months, younger cohort. UNCORRECTED (same data, same paper): younger cohort duration 18.9% SHORTER (coef -0.209), about 5.6 months EARLIER; older cohort not significant.
effects.evidence: the duration to first birth is longer among coresiding women by 16.2 % (= e0.150 - 1), or 4.6 months, for the older cohort and by 102.6 % (= e0.706 - 1), or 30.6 months, for the younger cohort
effects.note: RETRIEVED BY HAND 2026-08-28, AND THE MAGNITUDE IS LARGER THAN THE REVERSAL. The correction does not merely flip the sign: it moves the younger-cohort estimate from 5.6 months EARLIER to 30.6 months LATER, a swing of about three years in the timing of a first birth. The identification is a full-information maximum likelihood duration model with two endogenous binary decisions, excluding the husband's age at marriage from the duration equation; the authors report that excluded variable has substantial explanatory power in the co-residence equation. The bias direction is derived rather than asserted: traditional women both co-reside and give birth earlier, so a positive correlation between the two equations' unobservables biases the uncorrected estimate toward a shorter duration. This is the chapter's single most informative estimate.

effects.config_basis: none — the unit is a society, not a household
effects.arrangement_measure: prevalence of extended family structures in the society
effects.source_of_variation: historical crop suitability -> ancestral plough adoption, as an instrument
effects.estimate: +1.07 children per woman per SD of extended-family prevalence
effects.evidence: A one standard-deviation increase in prevalence of extended families is associated with approximately 1.07 additional children per woman.
effects.note: EXCLUDED FROM EVERY POOL, AND THE REASON IS THE SCOPE'S OWN WALL 3. The unit of observation is a society and the variation is cross-cultural, which is what Wall 3 rules out: societies with and without ancestral plough agriculture differ on everything the plough literature itself documents -- female labour force participation, gender norms, inheritance. The exclusion restriction requires plough adoption to affect fertility ONLY through family structure, and the adjacent literature is largely about the other channels. The magnitude, more than a full child per standard deviation, is on its own a reason to distrust it. Recorded rather than dropped, because a reader who finds it will want to know why it is not used.

effects.venue: Int. J. Geography, Geology and Environment
effects.config_basis: sample split, nuclear versus extended households
effects.estimate: 4.96 extended vs 4.65 nuclear; difference not significant
effects.evidence: Nuclear and extended family households showed no significant difference in mean number of children (4.65 versus 4.96, p>0.2).
effects.note: A NULL, and the only high-fertility-setting estimate in the cell. Small sample; the confidence interval is wide enough to contain the Vietnamese point estimate several times over.

effects.config_basis: co-residence and proximity measured separately in linked census data
effects.n: 3,173,297 couples linked; 2,047,694 in the net-reproduction models
effects.arrangement_measure: kin co-resident in household, and surname-kin density nearby
effects.estimate: co-resident mother IRR 0.951***; co-resident mother-in-law IRR 1.030***; nearby mother-in-law IRR 1.016***; adult surname-kin density IRR 1.283***
effects.direction: mixed — sign depends on WHICH kin
effects.evidence: Mother coresident in household 0.951 *** ... Mother-in-law coresident in household 1.030 *** ... Nearby mother-in-law 1.016 *** ... Adult surname kin density 1.283 ***
effects.note: THE CLEANEST EVIDENCE IN THE CHAPTER THAT THE EXPOSURE IS NOT ONE VARIABLE. In the same 3.1-million-couple dataset, a co-resident MOTHER lowers fertility 4.9% and a co-resident MOTHER-IN-LAW raises it 3.0%. Any estimate that averages 'living with a parent' averages across that. It is also the chapter's only FDT-era evidence, and the kin-density coefficient dwarfs both co-residence terms.

effects.venue: Vienna Institute of Demography Working Papers 03/2023
effects.estimate: association with desire for a second child; no association with third-child desire
effects.evidence: Multivariate regressions reveal an association between coresiding with parents and the desire for a second child, regardless of the sex of the first child. Among women with two children, third-child desires do not appear to be associated with coresiding with parents.
effects.note: Intentions. Pools only with intentions, per Ruling 4 stratum 2.

effects.venue: IZA DP 6651; B.E. Journal of Economic Analysis & Policy
effects.source_of_variation: difference-in-differences and regression discontinuity at the eligibility age threshold (22)
effects.anticipation_control: policy discontinuity at an age cutoff
effects.tempo_or_quantum: tempo (probability of at least one child, young ages)
effects.estimate: emancipation +0.9 to +2.3 pp; couple cohabitation +1.2 to +2.4 pp; probability of having children +4.8 to +8.1 pp (13-22% of the sample mean); no effect on marriage
effects.evidence: Difference-in-Differences and Regression Discontinuity estimates show that the policy increases emancipation rates by 0.9-2.3 percentage points, couple cohabitation by 1.2-2.4 percentage points, and the probability of having children by 4.8-8.1 percentage points for 22 year-olds compared to 21 year-olds.
effects.note: THE CHAPTER'S BEST DESIGN AND IT HAS A SPECIFIC, SERIOUS FLAW: the fertility effect is estimated CONDITIONAL ON BEING EMANCIPATED, and emancipation is itself moved by the treatment. Conditioning on a post-treatment variable, in a design whose whole point is that the treatment causes emancipation. The unconditional fertility effect is the estimand the chapter wants, and it is not the one reported.

effects.config_basis: young adults; not a co-residence measure
effects.setting: United States, state lotteries, universe of tax data 2000-2019
effects.arrangement_measure: homeownership and household formation (not co-residence directly)
effects.source_of_variation: lottery win, with future winners as an additional control group (triple difference)
effects.anticipation_control: randomised windfall; placebo pre-trends indistinguishable from zero
effects.tempo_or_quantum: BOTH, and that is the finding
effects.estimate: homeownership +5.59 pp per $100,000 at one year; total births at five years approximately zero, ruling out an increase above 0.01 children per $100,000
effects.evidence: One year after the lottery win, the effect of $100,000 is estimated to be 5.59 percentage points in the full sample ... Five years after the lottery win, the effect on total births is close to zero, and we can rule out an increase in the number of children of 0.01 per $100,000.
effects.note: NOT A CO-RESIDENCE ESTIMATE, AND IT BOUNDS THE CHAPTER ANYWAY. The exposure is an unconditional cash windfall, so it belongs to the income hypothesis. What it establishes is that pure liquidity moves the TIMING of births and not their number -- which is exactly the reading scope section 7 says the A.23 verdict turns on, arriving from the cleanest identification in the packet.

effects.venue: ECB WP 1910; Journal of Money, Credit and Banking
effects.source_of_variation: regional house-price variation, instrumented by predetermined local industrial structure
effects.tempo_or_quantum: tempo (a birth in the past year)
effects.estimate: Age 18-35 x change in 5-year house prices, 2006: had a child last year, 2SLS -0.0077 (SE 0.0050, p<0.10); OLS +0.0024 (SE 0.0030, not significant). Married, 2SLS -0.1140 (SE 0.0253). One standard deviation of house-price growth is 0.25, so one SD implies -0.19 percentage points on a 6% base (about -3.2% relative) for a birth, and -2.85 points on a 57% base for marriage. Young HOME OWNERS move the other way: Age 18-35 x Owner +0.0145.
effects.direction: negative for young non-owners; positive for young owners
effects.evidence: Age 18-35x 5-year house prices -0.0911*** -0.1140*** 0.0024 -0.0077* (0.0158) (0.0253) (0.0030) (0.0050) [Married OLS, Married 2SLS, Had a child OLS, Had a child 2SLS]
effects.note: RETRIEVED BY HAND 2026-08-28. TWO FINDINGS, AND THE SECOND WAS NOT VISIBLE IN THE ABSTRACT. First, the fertility effect is identified and SMALL: about -3.2% of the baseline probability of a birth per standard deviation of house-price growth, against -5.0% for marriage. Second, THE OLS AND THE IV DISAGREE IN SIGN - OLS gives +0.0024 and not significant, 2SLS gives -0.0077 and significant. That is the same estimator problem as Chu, arriving in a different literature with a different correction. The effect is also TENURE-CONDITIONAL: young owners become MORE likely to have a child when prices rise, which is C.2.c's finding that the aggregate elasticity is not a transportable parameter, reproduced here on the household-formation margin.

effects.evidence: We also found no evidence of significant effects on divorce, cohabitation, and fertility.
effects.note: A NULL FROM AN IDENTIFIED DESIGN, on a policy that does move living arrangements. One of the six designs Amendment 4 adds to scope section 4.

effects.venue: The Journal of the Economics of Ageing
effects.config_basis: pension eligibility of the ELDERLY parent
effects.setting: rural China, New Rural Pension Scheme
effects.source_of_variation: fuzzy regression discontinuity at the pension eligibility age
effects.estimate: adult sons co-residing with parents -0.389*** (Guizhou); grandchildren co-residing with grandparents -0.137*** (Guizhou); Shandong estimates insignificant
effects.evidence: Sample of adult sons Co-residing with parent(s) (Guizhou) 1016 -.389***(.081) ... Sample of the grandchildren from the sons' families Co-residing with grandparent(s) (Guizhou) 682 -.137***(.051)
effects.note: THE HOMONYM SITTING ON THE WALL, exactly as scope section 6 predicted. The exposure is a pension to the ELDERLY parent, which is the elder-support reading; the measured outcome includes GRANDCHILDREN co-residing with grandparents, which is the extended-couple reading. Same household, same dataset, two configurations. It is link 1 either way, since no fertility outcome is estimated, and it is the strongest available evidence that the arrangement responds to something exogenous.

effects.venue: Review of Economics of the Household
effects.source_of_variation: district variation in court inefficiency interacted with the reform
effects.evidence: household formation intentions = CourtIneff*Post = 0.0383*; fertility intentions = CourtIneff*Post = 0.0406**
effects.note: Intentions on both sides of the link, and the two coefficients are almost identical -- which is what the chapter would predict if the arrangement and the birth are governed by the same expectation rather than one causing the other.

effects.source_of_variation: cross-metro variation in affordability; Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition with a Heckman selection correction
effects.anticipation_control: selection model, not an exogenous shock
effects.estimate: up to a quarter of the 9-percentage-point rise in the co-residence share 2000-2021 attributed to declining affordability
effects.evidence: attribute up to a quarter of the observed 9-percentage-point increase in the co-residence share between 2000 and 2021 to a decrease in housing affordability
effects.note: THE EXPOSURE TREND'S BEST MAGNITUDE, and the input the demographic-significance section needs for the C.2.c-to-A.23 share. Not a fertility estimate.

effects.config_basis: life-course transitions of women, Spanish Fertility Survey 2018
effects.arrangement_measure: leaving the parental home (event and timing)
effects.estimate: association reported, no transportable magnitude extracted
effects.direction: positive (leaving home associated with higher probability of motherhood)
effects.evidence: Leaving the parental home also shows a strong association with the likelihood of motherhood, although it also appears to be mediated by the woman's economic, union, and employment status.
effects.note: THE AUTHORS STATE THE CHAPTER'S THREAT 1 THEMSELVES: 'it may be assumed that the desire to become a mother favours leaving home and co-residential union.' The association is real and it is not evidence about a direction. Included so the pre-launch cell is characterised rather than reported as empty.

effects.config_basis: none — the unit is a municipality
effects.arrangement_measure: household structure composition of the municipality
effects.evidence: la configuracion y la consolidacion de cierto tipo de hogares son capaces de explicar el comportamiento de la fecundidad o, en sentido contrario, los niveles de fecundidad pueden constituir un factor determinante para una tipologia especifica de hogar, esto implica ... un problema de la causalidad
effects.note: ECOLOGICAL, and the paper says in its own framing that the causal direction is a problem. Municipality-level household composition against municipality-level fertility. Recorded, not pooled.

effects.config_basis: children followed from age 15 into early adulthood
effects.setting: United States, PSID, federal subsidised housing
effects.n: about 1,700 black and 1,250 non-black individuals across the reported models
effects.arrangement_measure: cumulative years in public or privately managed subsidised housing; outcomes are teenage parenthood and forming an independent household
effects.source_of_variation: selection on observables with inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting, adjusting for length of stay and duration of eligibility
effects.anticipation_control: IPTW against the eligible-but-unhoused comparison group; NOT a randomised or administratively rationed allocation
effects.estimate: no effect on teenage parenthood for females; possibly a DECREASE for males; household formation possibly accelerated, but only into a subsidised apartment
effects.evidence: I find that the subsidized housing program has no effect on teenage parenthood for females but may decrease the probability of becoming a teenage parent for males. ... the subsidized housing program may accelerate the formation of households in early adulthood but only when that household is formed in a subsidized apartment.
effects.note: RETRIEVED BY HAND 2026-08-28, AND IT IS NOT THE DESIGN THE PACKET SAID IT WAS. The Wall 1 packet described it as administrative allocation of dwellings - the scope's design 3 - and treated it as a priority identified read. It is a selection-on-observables design with inverse-probability weighting against eligible non-recipients. That is a careful observational study, not a quasi-experiment, and it moves out of the identified count. Its fertility outcome is TEENAGE PARENTHOOD, a margin that cannot carry a completed-fertility verdict. The finding is a null, and the household-formation result is link 1: the programme changes WHERE a first independent household forms rather than whether young adults stay with their parents.

effects.config_basis: sample restriction — married couples who do and do not co-reside with the husband's parents
effects.source_of_variation: cross-section with propensity-score matching on the confounders of co-residence
effects.anticipation_control: propensity-score matching — balances OBSERVED confounders; it does not address unobserved anticipation
effects.estimate: positive and significant in the unmatched sample; reduced to NON-SIGNIFICANCE by the matching estimators. No point estimate extracted — full text not retrieved.
effects.evidence: coresidence with the husband's parents is positively associated with completed marital fertility in the unmatched sample ... However, the propensity score matching estimators show that this association is reduced to a non-significant level once the matching technique corrects the covariate imbalance.
effects.note: THE SECOND CORRECTED ESTIMATE, FOUND 2026-08-28, AND IT WAS ALREADY IN THIS CHAPTER'S OWN FRAME AT T1_primary_identified — never retrieved, recorded as `no_url` at stage 5b. It matters because it corrects the OTHER margin: Chu corrects a timing estimate and finds a thirty-month delay; Yoda corrects a COMPLETED FAMILY SIZE estimate and finds the positive association vanishing. Two corrections, two outcomes, and neither supports the positive association the uncorrected studies report. Weaker than Chu as identification — matching balances what is observed and cannot touch the anticipation problem scope §3 is about — so it is recorded as corrected for OBSERVED confounding and does not pool with Chu. Direction from the abstract; the article is closed at Taylor & Francis and the 2024 Routledge reprint is closed too.
